claims.text: Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported yield strength of 786 MPa.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a reported compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
Conventionally processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a terminal tensile strain of approximately 13.5%.
Existing evidence shows high impact-triggered energy release for HfZrTiTa0.53.
Heating HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 750°C for 2–4 hours constitutes a sub-solvus treatment.
The proposed treatment will induce fine secondary precipitation without appreciable grain growth.
The treatment will form fine, homogeneously distributed secondary precipitates at grain boundaries.
The secondary precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by the precipitates will reduce localized strain concentrations and promote more uniform plastic deformation.
The proposed microstructure will delay tensile necking.
At room temperature and a quasi-static tensile strain rate below 10^-3 s^-1, the treatment will increase tensile uniform elongation by approximately 50% or more relative to the stated 13.5% baseline.
The treated alloy will retain yield strength within ±10% of 786 MPa.
The treatment will cause no reduction in impact-triggered energy release.
The beneficial effect is expected specifically under room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
The treatment's effects at elevated temperatures and high strain rates are unverified.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is identified as terminal tensile strain, but it is then used as the baseline for uniform elongation. Terminal strain and uniform elongation are distinct tensile metrics, so the stated 50% comparison is not internally well matched.

The predicted outcome requires yield strength to remain within ±10% of 786 MPa, whereas the falsification rule addresses only a reduction greater than 10%. A strength increase exceeding 10% would violate the prediction but would not clearly trigger falsification.
